title: Reinforcement Learning Control for a Wave Energy Converter
kicker: Master's Project · Oregon State University · Energy Systems
tools: Python · Gymnasium · WEC-Sim (Wave Energy Converter Simulator) · MATLAB / Simulink · Stable-Baselines3 PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) · OSU HPC (Oregon State University high-performance computing) · W&B (Weights & Biases)
blurb: A Python interface that allows RL agents to control a full WEC-Sim simulation of a wave energy converter (WEC) step by step, matching a Simulink-only reference to ~1e-10. The follow-up project demonstrates that a PPO agent trained on a cheap linear model transfers to the full simulator with no degradation, but one thirtieth the training time.
long: A wave energy converter (WEC) converts the vertical movement of ocean waves into electricity. The one being analyzed, RM3 (Reference Model 3), is a buoy moving vertically on a tall spar. The generator connecting the two, the power take-off (PTO), exerts a force that pushes back on the buoy, and the selection of that force at each moment determines how much energy is harvested. The host research team at OSU (Oregon State University) controls the PTO by adjusting some damping parameters. RL could learn to control the force directly, however, the standard simulator, WEC-Sim is based on MATLAB and Simulink, without a Python API for controlling the system step by step.

The interface. wecsim_gym wraps WEC-Sim as a standard Gymnasium environment: the action is the PTO force, the observation is the float's position and velocity relative to the spar, the wave elevation (water-surface height at the device) and the previous action, and the reward is energy absorbed. Each episode is one free-running Simulink simulation that trades observations and forces with Python through shared memory in lockstep, with sequence numbers so no step can be skipped or repeated. Driven with a fixed damper, it matches the same control law built into Simulink without Python to about 1e-10 in mean power. A step takes 19.9 ms at a 0.1 s control step and 3.6 ms at 0.01 s on an HPC (high-performance computing) node. Five RL libraries (Stable-Baselines3, RLlib, Tianshou, TorchRL, CleanRL) train on it unchanged, and 11 MATLAB integration tests pass.

Cheap model versus full simulator. The side study compared WEC-Sim to the group’s 10-state linear model of the same WEC, which runs in a few microseconds rather than 20 ms per timestep. Given the same wave forces, they behave nearly identically (≥0.9985 correlation for three different wave seeds), with the linear model extracting a steady 6.7–7.8% less power. We trained PPO agents on each simulation and tested them in both: the agent trained on the linear model achieved an average power of 148.8 kW in WEC-Sim, This is level with the best tuned fixed damper (147.4 kW) and above WEC-Sim’s example damper (113.8 kW). The agent took 2.4 minutes to train, instead of 71 minutes.

Both agents learned almost the same policy of a near-tuned linear damper instead of learning something novel, this is expected for a single sea state because a fixed damper can be tuned for that sea-state. The next step is to train over many sea-states, where a fixed damper cannot. As they were learning they replicated two figures from the group’s previous paper, this revealed that their wave generator was providing ~22% less wave energy compared to WEC-Sim at the same nominal wave height. They are validating against the references which were written by the creators of WEC-Sim.
highlights: Gymnasium interface matches a Simulink-only reference to ~1e-10 in mean power
19.9 ms per 0.1 s control step on an HPC (high-performance computing) node; 5 RL (reinforcement learning) libraries train unchanged
PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) trained on a linear model: 148.8 kW on WEC-Sim vs 147.4 kW tuned damper, in 2.4 min instead of 71
Linear model vs WEC-Sim motion correlation ≥ 0.9985 across three wave seeds
